transcript:
Header: 2027-12-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (FinSight - Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (FinSight - Infra), Samantha Li (FinSight - Platform PM)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is our weekly poc sync so want to run through the throughput numbers we ran last night and then decide next tuning steps. liam, you want to start with the quick recap?
[00:18] Liam: yeah sure. quick recap — we ran two experiments overnight. baseline was your current config: concurrency 16, batching window 8ms, no prefix caching; second was tuned: concurrency 48, continuous batching enabled with 20ms window, and small KV prefix cache warmed for common prompts. results were, like, broadly — throughput up ~2.8x, p50 stable, p95 up a bit, p99 increased on heavier tails.
[00:42] Priya: can you give numbers? our data scientists will want exact qps and latency percentiles.
[00:47] Liam: absolutely. baseline sustained about 800 reqs/min at concurrency 16. tuned run hit steady 2,300 to 2,450 reqs/min depending on minibatch packing, we saw p50 around 120ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 spiking toward 1.2s on some long-context samples. there was one outlier where the kv-cache miss pattern triggered longer sequences and p99 jumped.
[01:15] Ethan: interesting. what about tokenization differences? our payloads have variable-length prompts, sometimes long system context which could affect batching.
[01:24] Liam: yep, we noticed variance. continuous batching helps by grouping similar sequence lengths, but when you get long tails it penalizes p99. we proposed two mitigations: adaptive batching thresholds (to avoid mixing very long sequences) and a small concurrent queue with priority for short/latency-sensitive requests.
[01:43] Maya: to add, routing policies can also help — you can route critical low-latency traffic to a low-concurrency pool and bulk infer to a high-throughput pool. that's where Dedicated routing or per-route configs come in.
[01:55] Samantha: quick question — how does that affect cost? if we bump concurrency from 16 to 48 we reduce cost per token but does it increase infra spend due to p99 tail?
[02:05] Liam: tradeoff. higher concurrency and better batching reduces tokens/second CPU/GPU overhead and amortizes kernel launches; cost per token goes down. however, if you need to hold a bigger instance pool to keep p99 tight you might see infra cost rising. in our internal sims, for FinSight's workload, optimized batching reduced estimated token costs by ~32% while infra hours increased marginally due to higher util, so net savings.
[02:34] Priya: can you show the sheet?
[02:36] Maya: yes i will send the updated benchmark sheet after this call. it includes concurrency vs qps vs latency columns and cost estimates.
[02:43] Liam: also note we tested a fallback policy: when queue length exceeds threshold we route to smaller model variant — lower quality but faster — that helped keep tail latencies bounded. worth discussing if FinSight can accept lower-quality fallbacks for non-critical paths.
[03:02] Priya: for customer-facing features we can't have lower-grade answers, but for internal batch analytics it's ok. we'll flag which endpoints are eligible.
[03:12] Ethan: about queueing — can you explain the backpressure model briefly? we saw a little jitter when we bumped concurrency, curious how Redwood defers incoming requests.
[03:20] Liam: sure. current model uses an in-memory request queue per worker. we maintain a soft concurrency target; if active slots exceed target we hold new requests for up to a short timeout and try again to pack into the next batch. there is optional client-side retry/backoff and server-side queue length thresholds which trigger routing to auxiliary pools or fallbacks. the important knobs are: max_concurrency, batch_window_ms, max_queue_ms, and queue_strategy (fifo/priority).
[03:49] Samantha: can we get recommended values? e.g. for a p95 of 400ms target and average prompt length x tokens?
[03:58] Liam: yeah recommended starting point for your traffic profile — avg prompt 180 tokens — is concurrency 48, batch window 15–25ms, max_queue_ms 120ms, and priority queue for < 128-token requests. that should hit p95 sub-500ms in most cases. we'll tune further once we have real traffic sampler.
[04:18] Priya: KMS / security checkpoint — last week we asked about KMS integration and audit logs for private deployments. where are we on that?
[04:26] Maya: we will share the SOC2 whitepaper and the KMS/HSM integration doc. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption and a bring-your-key option. i'll attach the security pack.
[04:39] Ethan: any blockers for VPC peering? we need to schedule a maintenance window with infra to set up peering to their VPC in us-east-1.
[04:47] Liam: no blockers from Redwood side; we just need the network ranges and a preferred 2-hour window.
[04:54] Samantha: timeline — we'd like to be in pilot production by mid-december. is that realistic?
[05:00] Maya: yes — if we get the traffic sampler and we run two more tuning iterations this week, and you confirm peering and security sign-off, mid-december pilot looks doable.
[05:10] Priya: ok let's talk about one of the weird errors we saw — intermittent 502s when concurrency spiked. is that queuing overflow or infra flakiness?
[05:19] Liam: likely queuing overflow on the ingress side — we saw delayed handshakes causing worker-side timeouts. we'll increase the queue timeout slightly and instrument with more trace IDs for the next run. i'll also include the logs in the artifact we'll share.
[05:33] Maya: quick note — when you run the benchmark against your staging traffic, try two scenarios: steady-state QPS and spikey burst profile (30% of traffic in 1 minute) so we can surface tail behavior.
[05:45] Ethan: will do. what about autoscaling? if we see sustained qps above predicted, how quickly does Redwood Dedicated scale?
[05:53] Liam: Dedicated supports configured autoscaling policies: scale-up ramp in minutes, and burst capacity options you can enable to bring extra instances for short spikes. if you need sub-minute scaling we can pre-warm instances or use a burst pool. there are tradeoffs: burst pool costs more but keeps tails short.
[06:10] Priya: can you run a simulation with our traffic sampler and show cost vs p95 for both Hosted and Dedicated?
[06:16] Maya: yes we'll include that in the benchmark spreadsheet — separate tabs for Hosted vs Dedicated with cost modelling.
[06:22] Samantha: last question from my side — observational hooks: can we get per-route token-level cost breakdown in the console? we need to map features to spend.
[06:31] Maya: console supports per-route dashboards and tracing; we can enable token-level breakdown for your account and add the specific routes you care about.
[06:38] Liam: one more technical note — we observed that enabling int8 quantization for this model reduced per-token latency slightly but introduced a 3–5% quality delta on some classification tasks. we flagged which prompts are sensitive in the results doc.
[06:52] Priya: that's helpful — we'll review prompts and mark the sensitive ones.
[06:57] Maya: ok recap of next steps — maya to send updated sheet + security docs; liam to tweak batching and share logs; ethan to provide traffic sampler and peering window; schedule next tuning run fri?
[07:11] Samantha: fri works for us, afternoon prefer 3pm east.
[07:16] Maya: i'll propose calendar invite for 2027-12-04 15:00 ET.
[07:20] Priya: thanks all.

[07:25] — End of recording —
